output.content:
The street was not on any map in the Survey Office until it was.

Miriam Das had said that aloud to the wall of her attic room above the printing press in Bowbazar, and the wall had not answered, which was a relief. The monsoon had come early and thin, a weeping that left the tin roof ticking. Below, the pressmen were setting type for the *Calcutta Gazette*. The smell of ink and hot metal rose through the floorboards.

She was thirty-four, a widow, and the first woman the Great Trigonometrical Survey had permitted to work indoors. Not in the field — the men were careful about that — but at the table. Ink, paper, copper plates, and the endless sheets of field notes brought in from the mofussil by sweating bearers. She was the one who made them legible.

On her table lay the Ward No. 7 revision for 1893. Boral Lane to College Square was accounted for. The new tramline was marked in red pencil. The Municipal Corporation had asked for a clean sheet by month’s end for the tax collector.

She took her steel nib, dipped, and began to trace the line she had walked that morning to verify. Kumartuli Gali, narrow and good. The sweetmeat shops. The lane that led to the ghat where the idol-makers worked. All true.

Her pen stopped at a gap.

Between the lane of the potters and the lane of the vegetable sellers there should have been a short connecting thoroughfare the previous year: Sutanuti Lane. She had mapped it herself in 1891. She remembered the name because it was absurd. Sutanuti was the old name for the whole city.

The lane was gone from the new surveyor’s notes. The new surveyor, Mr. Hargreaves, had crossed it out with a single neat line and written *closed — private*. Yet the tax records still listed twenty-one houses on Sutanuti Lane. The municipal lamp-post register listed three lamps.

Miriam pulled down the 1889 survey from the stack. There it was. A little finger of a street, one hundred and twelve feet long, running south off Chitpur Road. She remembered it because the surveyor’s note in the margin read: *narrow, stinking, children playing with broken boats*.

She lifted the 1893 field book. No entry. Hargreaves had written in his crabbed hand: *Lane not found. Local informant claims it moved.*

She stared at the word. Moved.

That evening she went out before dusk, with her notebook and a lantern she did not intend to light. The air was heavy, yellow with smoke from the brick kilns. She walked from the office on Harrison Road to Chitpur. She knew the way by her own feet.

Chitpur Road was a roar. Bullock carts, cycle-rickshaws, a procession of marwari merchants arguing over jute prices. The smell of fish from the ghats, the smell of coal, the smell of humanity pressed too close.

She found the potters’ lane. She found the vegetable sellers. Between them the wall was solid, a brick wall with a wooden gate painted green and padlocked. A brass nameplate above the gate read: *Sutanuti Lane — Private Residence of Babu K. N. Mukherjee*.

No. That wasn’t right. There had been shops. A tea stall. A child with a broken boat.

She knocked. A maidservant in a faded sari opened a crack and stared.

“Madam?”

“I am from the Survey. I am looking for the lane.”

The maidservant did not smile. “This is the lane, madam.”

“But the map—”

“The map is wrong last year.”

“May I walk through?”

The maidservant considered this as if it were a strange request. “Babu says the lane opens at five in the morning. For milkmen. After that, it closes.”

Miriam wrote that down.

At the office at nine the next morning, Hargreaves was already there, mopping his forehead with a handkerchief. He was a man of forty, thin as a heron, and proud of his discretion. He took off his pith helmet.

“Miss Das,” he said. “You were out late?”

“Verifying Sutanuti Lane.”

He sighed. “I told you. It’s a dead end now. Mukherjee bought the frontage and bricked it. The Corporation will thank me for cleaning the map.”

“He told a maid it opens at five for milkmen.”

Hargreaves laughed, a dry sound. “They all say things. You cannot put every superstition on a map, Miss Das.”

“I put what is.”

“You put what you can prove. And you cannot enter the lane after five because the gate is locked.”

“Then I will enter before five.”

That night she lay awake listening to the roof. At three o’clock she rose, dressed in a plain cotton sari, took her notebook, and walked in darkness without lantern. The city was different then. The river breathed. Dogs moved like shadows. The tramcars were still.

She reached Chitpur before four. The lane was there. The gate was open, not padlocked, the green paint dark in the pre-dawn. No sign of Mukherjee’s house. Instead the wall was nothing, an opening, and beyond it a street she recognized from the 1889 map: Sutanuti Lane, narrow as a throat, the potters’ lane on one side, the vegetable sellers on the other, exactly as she remembered. A tea stall with a flickering oil lamp. A boy with a broken boat.

She stepped in.

For a moment she was afraid to breathe. The street smelled of wet earth and clay and the river. A milkman passed with his tin can balancing on his head, nodding to her as if she belonged. The houses on either side were unremarkable, brick and wood, with laundry strung across. The numbers were there: 1 to 21. She counted. She wrote it down by the light of the tea stall.

At five exactly, a bell rang somewhere far off. The milkman turned his cart. The gate behind her creaked shut on its own.

She stepped back out onto Chitpur Road and looked down the street. The opening was gone. In its place was the green gate and the nameplate for Babu K. N. Mukherjee. The wall was solid.

Miriam stood there with her notebook open, her fingers ink-stained, staring at a street that had been there and was not there.

She walked home fast, too fast for a respectable woman, and went straight to her attic. She spread the 1893 sheet on the table. She drew the lane in with a firm, black line, then looked at the field notes and added in the margin in her own hand: *Lane exists 04:00 to 05:00 only. Verified 18 August 1893.*

She had to be certain it was not a trick of sleep. She needed a witness. The next morning at the Survey Office she asked for the youngest boy, Ramesh, who ran messages.

“Will you come with me tonight?” she asked.

He looked up, eyes wide. “Madam, it is not safe.”

“It is safe if we are together. I will pay you two annas.”

He nodded.

They went at four-forty-five. The city was waking. The gate was locked. Ramesh fidgeted.

“Wait,” she said.

At four-fifty-nine they stood. The bell rang. The gate gave a sigh and the lock fell open. The street was there.

Ramesh gasped. “Ma… Madam… where did this come from?”

Miriam walked in first. The milkman passed them again, same tin can, same nod.

Ramesh whispered, “I have never seen this before.”

“Now you have.”

They walked the length of the lane and back. At five-oh-one the tea stall lamp went out. The houses seemed to exhale. At five-oh-two the gate began to close. The wall rose like a curtain.

Ramesh grabbed her sleeve. “We must run!”

They ran.

On Chitpur Road the wall was whole.

Back in the attic, Miriam laid out three sheets: 1889, 1893, and her own sketch with the time annotation. She stared at the empty space on the 1893 revision where the lane should be. Hargreaves had crossed it out. She would have to put it back.

The ink was still wet when a soft knock came at her door downstairs. The pressmen were gone for the day. She opened the attic stair and found a boy standing there, barefoot, holding a broken wooden boat.

He was the boy from the lane.

“You are the map lady,” he said.

She did not know what to say. “Yes.”

“The street doesn’t like being mapped,” he said.

Miriam’s throat was dry. “What does it do?”

“It moves. Every night it walks a little further, so no one can find it in the day. If you put it on paper, it will know you can follow.”

She looked down at her notebook where the lane was drawn in ink. The pen had left a smear. The smear had formed a shape she had not intended — a tiny dot off the end of the lane, a door that was not there before.

The boy smiled sadly. “The door is new. It wasn’t there last night.”

Before she could ask what the door was for, the roof ticked louder and the monsoon came in with a sudden, hard rain that beat the tin like a drum. When the knocking came again, louder this time, it was not at her door but at the window of the attic, where the rain could not reach.

She turned. The window was open a crack. And through it, in the wet dark, she could see the green gate of Sutanuti Lane, standing there in the middle of her room, its narrow wooden slats reflecting the lamplight, the padlock glinting, and beyond it a street that existed only between four and five in the morning — and now it was standing in her attic at midnight, waiting for her to step through.
